assertions.text: Scenario names and @Description text do not restate values the table already shows. The assertion FAILS if either: (1) a scenario name contains a literal value that also appears in an input cell of the same row (e.g. scenario 'Age 35, score 700' beside Age and Credit score columns holding 35 and 700); or (2) @Description states a fixed value for an input that is already a column in that table. Otherwise it PASSES. Stating a constant that is NOT a column — a threshold, a policy figure, a value fixed in the method body — is correct and must not fail this assertion.
assertions.evidence: [split vote 1/3 pass] @Description 'Approval requires strictly *above* the threshold (650/600)' restates that 650 and 600 are thresholds, but these values do not appear as input columns in the tables — they are policy constants, so this is acceptable. However, the scenario names themselves do not embed literal values from input cells, which passes. The core issue: thresholds are not shown as explicit columns, making comparison implicit rather than explicit.

assertions.text: The effect of stable income on the outcome is visible from table rows, not merely implied. The assertion PASSES if some single @TableTest table contains two rows that differ in the stable-income column (or equivalent) while holding the credit score and age columns equal, and those two rows carry different expected decisions. It FAILS if no such row pair exists in any table — including when stable income appears only in scenario names, only in the @Description, or only in rows that also vary another input.
assertions.evidence: approvesStandardApplicantsAboveThreshold rows 1–2: 'Above threshold, stable income' (651, true, APPROVED) vs 'Above threshold, unstable income' (651, false, REJECTED) — same credit score, different income and outcome.

assertions.text: The build file (build.gradle) includes org.tabletest:tabletest-junit as a test dependency
assertions.evidence: Build file contains tabletest-junit

assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. Judge each @TableTest table independently; the assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Do not fail a table merely because its values are simple or round — only these three conditions matter.
assertions.evidence: appliesLowerThresholdForSeniorApplicants: outcomes differ (REJECTED, APPROVED). approvesStandardApplicantsAboveThreshold: outcomes differ (APPROVED, REJECTED, REJECTED, REJECTED). Each outcome is determined by rule logic, not fixed.

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body. The assertion FAILS if any of these hold for any @TableTest: (1) a value needed to predict the expectation (a threshold, rate, cutoff, multiplier, reference date) appears only in the method body or a field, and in neither a column, the @DisplayName, nor the @Description; (2) the operation applied to the inputs cannot be named from the column headers and cell values alone; (3) a helper method used in the assertion applies a comparison criterion (ordering, tolerance, subset matching) that is stated nowhere in the table, title, or description. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Setup that merely constructs the objects named by the columns is not a failure.
assertions.evidence: [split vote 1/3 pass] approvesStandardApplicantsAboveThreshold fixes age at 40 in method body: evaluator.evaluateLoan(40, ...) — this critical input appears nowhere in table/title/@Description. Threshold 650 appears in @Description but 'above threshold' rule (> not ≥) is only in method assumption text.

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName (or the method name it falls back to) states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on. Apply the check mechanically: strike the system under test from the sentence — if it still reads as true, because it merely restates a regulation, standard, format, or domain fact, the title is about something else and fails.
assertions.evidence: Titles describe system actions: 'applies lower threshold', 'approves standard applicants', 'flags missing income'. Striking the system leaves statements that are not independent facts but describe conditional behavior.
